question: A researcher uploaded a single industry report and asked for a summary of it. Web search was switched off throughout. Which observation is the strongest sign that a detail in the summary was fabricated rather than drawn from the report?
options: A) The summary opens with general background about the industry before it turns to the specific findings the report contains.
B) The summary is noticeably longer than the researcher expected for a report of this size, and repeats one point in two places.
C) The summary states a precise figure, with a named source and a year, that appears nowhere in the uploaded report itself.
D) The summary uses phrasing of its own rather than reusing the exact sentences that appear in the uploaded industry report.
correct_answers: C) The summary states a precise figure, with a named source and a year, that appears nowhere in the uploaded report itself.
explanations: General framing before the specifics is a stylistic choice and is easy to remove. It becomes a concern only if the background contains checkable claims, which is not what this observation describes.
Length and repetition point to a shape-and-quality problem rather than an invention problem. A verbose or redundant summary can still be entirely faithful to the document it was built from.

Correct. With no web search and a single uploaded document, everything factual should trace back to that document. A precise, confidently attributed figure that is absent from the source is the classic signature of fabricated detail.

Paraphrasing is normal and often desirable in a summary; different wording says nothing about whether the underlying content came from the report. This would flag almost every competent summary as suspect.
